title: Revolut Targets Broader Technology Expansion as AI and Banking Services Converge
excerpt: Revolut Targets Broader Technology Expansion as AI and Banking Services Converge. LONDON, United Kingdom, Revolut is positioning itself for a broader role in the technology industry, with Chief Executive Nik Storonsky outlining ambitions to expand beyond traditional financial services. The European fintech company is exploring how its large volume of customer transaction data and artificial intelligence capabilities could support new products as it continues expanding internationally. Speaking at a technology forum in Turin, Italy, on October 9, Storonsky said Revolut processes approximately 30 million to 40 million transactions each day. The company is using its data resources to develop proprietary AI models, with ambitions to build a business operating at a scale comparable to major US technology companies. The strategy signals a potential shift for a company originally built around digital payments and banking services, as fintech businesses increasingly look to diversify their products and revenue streams. Transaction Data Becomes a Technology Asset. Financial transactions generate information about spending patterns, payment behaviour and the ways customers interact with financial services. When handled under appropriate privacy, security and regulatory safeguards, this information can help financial institutions improve fraud detection, personalize services and automate certain processes. Revolut’s transaction volume provides a substantial data resource for developing financial technology products. Its interest in proprietary AI models reflects a wider industry trend in which banks and fintech companies are exploring how machine learning can improve customer experiences and internal operations. However, financial data is particularly sensitive. Any effort to build AI powered services must account for data protection requirements, model security and the potential consequences of inaccurate automated decisions. The commercial opportunity will depend on whether these tools deliver measurable benefits while maintaining customer trust. International Expansion Remains Central. Revolut has continued pursuing regulatory approvals and broader market access. In September 2026, the company received preliminary approval for a national banking licence in the United States, following banking licence developments in the United Kingdom and France earlier in the year. Such approvals can create opportunities to expand products and serve customers under different regulatory frameworks, although preliminary approval is not equivalent to unrestricted operating authorization. Each market brings its own requirements for capital, governance, consumer protection and financial crime controls. Revolut’s ambition to move beyond banking will therefore develop alongside its existing regulatory responsibilities. Expanding into additional technology services could also require new expertise, investment and partnerships. Regulatory Challenges Could Shape Growth. The company’s expansion comes with scrutiny over its control systems. Lithuania’s central bank imposed a €3. 5 million fine on Revolut in 2025 over deficiencies in transaction monitoring. In September 2026, the company also disclosed an incident in which customer data was mistakenly sent to individuals posing as government investigators. These incidents highlight the importance of strong safeguards as fintech companies grow. Rapid product development and international expansion must be supported by effective financial crime monitoring, data protection and internal controls. The Outlook for Fintech Competition. Revolut’s strategy reflects a broader question facing digital financial platforms: whether their customer relationships and technology infrastructure can support businesses extending well beyond payments and banking. title: World Bank: African languages are underrepresented in Artificial Intelligence
excerpt: World Bank: African languages are underrepresented in Artificial Intelligence. Sunday 11th October, 2026 01:33 AM | By Aloys Michael. As artificial intelligence (AI) transforms education, business and access to information, millions of Africans risk being left behind if the technology cannot adequately understand the languages they speak. The World Bank has identified the underrepresentation of African languages, institutions and economic activities in AI training data as a barrier to developing systems that respond effectively to the continent’s needs. In its Africa Economic Update: Building AI Readiness , published in October 2026, the bank warns that gaps in global datasets can limit the contextual performance of AI models. “Global training data sets substantially underrepresent African countries, languages, institutions, and economic activities,” the report says. The concern is significant for a continent with approximately 2,000 languages. Although AI tools can generate text, answer questions and support decision-making, their usefulness depends partly on how well they understand different languages and cultural contexts. The challenge is therefore not simply whether Africans can access AI, but whether the technology can serve them reliably in the languages they use. The language gap in AI. According to the World Bank, an estimated 56 per cent of open-source training data is exclusively in English. This imbalance raises concerns about the ability of AI systems to serve people who communicate in languages with fewer digital resources. AI models learn patterns from training data. When high-quality material in a particular language is scarce, developers may have fewer resources to train and evaluate systems for that language. This can affect tasks such as translation, answering questions and interpreting local expressions. The consequences could extend to everyday services. Farmers may need agricultural advice using familiar terminology, students may benefit from learning materials in their preferred languages, and health workers may require clear communication tools for patients. These are potential applications rather than proof that AI systems consistently fail in African languages. Performance varies by language, model and task, making independent testing essential. Building AI around African needs. The World Bank argues that adapting AI to local conditions offers significant opportunities for Sub-Saharan African countries. “The deepest returns for Sub-Saharan African countries lie in adapting AI to local data, languages, and problems,” the report says. One example is InkubaLM, a small language model developed by African AI company Lelapa AI. According to the World Bank, it was trained on five African languages: isiZulu, Yoruba, Hausa, Swahili and isiXhosa. The report says the model reportedly outperforms much larger models on those languages. The example illustrates how specialised models focused on local languages could complement larger, general-purpose AI systems. However, performance claims depend on the benchmarks and tasks evaluated. Success in selected tests does not automatically mean a model performs better in every real-world application. Expanding these efforts requires quality language datasets, skilled researchers, sustainable funding and computing resources. Developers must also test their systems with actual users to determine whether they understand questions correctly and provide reliable answers. Who owns Africa’s language data?. Developing African-language AI also raises questions about how language data is collected, controlled and used. Building datasets may require written materials, speech recordings, translations and contributions from local researchers and communities. Clear rules are needed to establish permission for data use, protect privacy and determine how contributors are recognised or compensated where appropriate. title: AI accelerates Korea bank hacks by automating attacks on shadow IT - CHOSUNBIZ
excerpt: By Lee Jae-eun. Published 2026. 10. 08. 14:26 Updated 2026. 10. 08. 14:35. Prefer Chosunbiz EN on Google. A recent hacking incident in the financial sector was not about artificial intelligence (AI) inventing new attack techniques but rather automating and advancing existing ones, according to an analysis. It said hackers abused AI-based tools to target security blind spots where corporations' management was weak. The white-hat hacker team EQST at SK shieldus stated accordingly on Jan. 8 in a report titled "The era of AI-automated attacks: Incident analysis and response guide targeting shadow IT," which outlined how the artificial intelligence (AI) attack tool "ARTEX," reportedly used in the financial sector hacks, operates and the risks it poses. ARTEX is an open-source autonomous penetration testing platform that automates the human-led red-teaming process with AI. It selects the next reconnaissance target on its own based on prior results and can expand attack paths. SK shieldus analyzed, "This structure automated the attacker's reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, and validation processes, increasing the speed and scope of attacks. " Based on currently available information and tool analysis, it also said, "It is possible the attacker used publicly available AI-based penetration testing tools to route through virtual private servers (VPS) in multiple countries and probe internet-exposed services and application programming interfaces (API) of multiple financial firms. ". In this financial sector breach as well, the hacker appeared to prioritize externally exposed systems that fell into management blind spots—such as the loan broker system, employee support services, and sales support platforms—over core financial transaction systems. When using AI-based automated attack tools, an attacker can simultaneously probe internet-exposed assets and APIs of multiple financial institutions and rapidly expand targets by analyzing API call patterns and response data. The attack likewise proceeded along existing steps—scanning for externally exposed assets, identifying authentication and authorization vulnerabilities, mass queries, blocking evasion, and propagation to other institutions. SK shieldus assessed, "AI automated these attack processes, amplifying their speed and scale. ". Review Costco 1 Oz Gold Bar Pricing And Buying Considerations (Search Now) FAQArena | Costco Gold Bar. SK shieldus identified "shadow IT" as the starting point of such AI-driven attacks. It refers to external touchpoints that operate outside the inventory and control of a corporation's security organization. It includes not only assets whose existence is unknown but also those known yet pushed down the management priority list and thus poorly inspected. The company said, "This incident shows that the essence of AI attacks is not discovering new vulnerabilities but finding and exploiting unmanaged assets more quickly," adding, "In particular, because APIs concentrate corporations' business logic and data access paths, if AI analyzes them, activities such as mass queries, authorization bypass attempts, and expansion of abnormal calls can occur more efficiently. ". It also emphasized that securing asset visibility is paramount to respond to AI-based automated attacks. Since AI can rapidly discover internet-exposed APIs and vulnerable assets, it argued that corporations must accurately identify and manage the assets they hold. SK shieldus said, "You cannot protect assets you do not know, and you cannot control calls you cannot see," adding, "Only after asset identification is complete can you define inspection targets, and only with inspection criteria can you build effective detection and response systems. ". title: Over half of HK entrepreneurs see AI as catalyst for workforce growth: HSBC
excerpt: Hong Kong Racing. World Racing. Analysis. Racecourse Entertainment. Lifestyle. Arts & Culture. Wellness. Food & Wine. Leisure. Showbiz. Entertainment. Gossip. Screen & Music. Sport. Sports Updates. Football. Basketball. Tennis. Opinion. Editorial. Insights. Games. Crossword. BUSINESS. FINANCE. Over half of HK entrepreneurs see AI as catalyst for workforce growth: HSBC. FINANCE. 29-09-2026 15:24 HKT. by. Gloria Leung. Hong Kong entrepreneurs are banking on artificial intelligence for future growth, leading the global average, with 58 percent expecting AI adoption to increase headcount over the next two years, according to HSBC’s latest report. HSBC Private Bank's Global Entrepreneurial Wealth Report 2026 surveyed over 3,000 high net worth (HNW) and ultra-high net worth (UHNW) entrepreneurs and founders worldwide. It found that 69 percent of Hong Kong entrepreneurs plan to invest between 11 percent and 30 percent of their annual turnover in AI technologies over the next 12 months, compared with 61 percent globally. Meanwhile, 55 percent believe AI will improve productivity, compared with 43 percent globally, and 39 percent believe it will help identify new markets and business opportunities. Notably, 98 percent of entrepreneurs in Hong Kong are highly optimistic about their business prospects and personal wealth, compared with 95 percent globally, with more than half describing themselves as "very positive", compared with 49 percent globally. In addition, 91 percent expect their personal wealth to improve in the coming years, including 53 percent who expect it will get "a lot better", compared with 44 percent globally. Despite embracing AI, 42 percent of Hong Kong entrepreneurs cited integrating the technology into legacy systems, and 41 percent pointed to employee resistance as among their biggest concerns. “AI is a key driver of confidence, as business owners invest in technology to stay ahead of disruption. But technology alone can’t deliver sustained success,” said Lok Yim, regional head of HSBC Private Bank, Asia Pacific, noting that the best strategy is to combine investment, connections, foresight, and risk management to turn opportunity into long-term growth. The report also highlighted that 77 percent of Hong Kong entrepreneurs plan to expand with an additional residency abroad. Singapore and Japan are among their most popular destinations. When asked about Hong Kong businesses’ regional growth ambition, over 40 percent of them chose mainland China and Singapore to expand their businesses, followed by the US, India, and the UK. Another key finding pointed to optimism in the next generation of females, with 74 percent of the UHNW women aged 18 to 34 believing their wealth will get a lot better, compared with the global average of 44 percent. title: Regulations on safety and risk management for the application of AI in banking.
excerpt: . Regulations on safety and risk management for the application of AI in banking. The State Bank of Vietnam has recently issued Circular No. 53/2026/TT-NHNN regulating safety, risk management, and deployment conditions for the application of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in the banking industry. Notably, the new regulations set forth a series of requirements directly related to customer rights, ranging from notifying customers when they are interacting with AI, explaining automated decisions, allowing human review in case of complaints, to tightly controlling payment transactions and credit granting decisions made by AI. Thời báo Ngân hàng • 07/10/2026. This circular applies to credit institutions, branches of foreign banks, payment intermediary service providers, credit information companies, mobile money service providers, and several other entities in the banking sector. The scope of regulation covers the use of AI in banking, payment intermediary, credit information, and mobile money operations. A key principle established by the State Bank of Vietnam is that AI does not replace human authority and responsibility. Service providers remain legally and customer-accountable for decisions or decisions supported by AI systems. Organizations are prohibited from invoking the technical characteristics, autonomy of the system, or the use of third-party products to exclude or reduce managerial and legal liability. This is noteworthy as banks increasingly incorporate AI into scoring, advising, customer care, fraud prevention, and business process automation. According to the Circular, before deployment, AI systems must be classified according to risk level: high, medium, or low. Specifically in the banking sector, some automated systems that perform electronic transactions or automatically suggest credit approval decisions may be classified as high-risk. Classification of AI system risks in the banking industry. Design: Hong Son Specifically, AI-powered automated payment transaction systems are classified as high-risk if they process transactions for individual customers exceeding 10 million VND or if the total daily transaction value for a single customer exceeds 20 million VND. For institutional clients, the corresponding thresholds are over 50 million VND per transaction or over 100 million VND per day. AI-powered automated credit approval systems are also considered high-risk if the credit amount is 50 million VND or more. For AI to automate payment transactions, banks and customers must have a prior agreement. This agreement must clearly define the scope of transactions to be automated, the limits for each transaction and per day, the validity period, applicable conditions, the customer's right to terminate the agreement at any time, and the responsibility of the AI ​​unit to immediately fulfill the termination request. The circular also sets limits on the size of transactions that AI can automatically execute. The total value of transactions in a day must not exceed the internal limit of the service provider and must not exceed VND 100 million for individual customers and VND 500 million for institutional customers. Customers must also have tools to proactively pause or cancel AI's authorization to automatically execute payment transactions. You may also like. Along with transaction control requirements, the new regulations emphasize the possibility of human intervention. The supervisory body must have sufficient authority and capability to override, modify, or pause AI decisions, or activate emergency shutdown mechanisms when necessary. Any interference with system decisions must be documented, including the content, time, person performing the intervention, and reason for the intervention. From a customer protection perspective, one key concern is the requirement for transparency when using AI for communication or decision-making. title: Developer shutters AI tool tied to Korean bank hacks
excerpt: . SEOUL, October 10 (AJP) - ARTEX, a Chinese AI penetration-testing tool linked to a string of breaches at South Korean banks, is going closed-source and will receive no further updates, its developer said. “Given the misuse of the tool, the ARTEX project will no longer be updated and will be converted to closed source,” the developer, known as Autumn-27, said in a GitHub post on Oct. 8. The developer added that no new versions would be released to the public. The developer said ARTEX was built to help organizations test their defenses and disclaimed responsibility for any illegal use, without referring to the attacks in Korea. The project’s GitHub page has since been taken down. U. S. cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said on Oct. 7 that a financially motivated actor, likely a Chinese speaker, ran ARTEX on a DeepSeek model to target South Korean financial institutions between late September and early October. Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Hana Bank have reported customer data leaks, with Shinhan alone exposing information on about 25,000 customers. NH NongHyup Bank and Woori Bank fended off the intrusions. The shutdown covers only future versions. A Korean-language translation of ARTEX, with added detection rules, surfaced on GitHub on Wednesday, a day before the announcement. AJP Takeaways - The Chinese developer of ARTEX, an AI penetration-testing tool linked to attacks on South Korean banks, said on Oct. 8, 2026 that the project will go closed-source and get no further updates. - CrowdStrike said on Oct. 7, 2026 that a likely Chinese-speaking, financially motivated actor used ARTEX with a DeepSeek model against South Korean financial institutions from late September to early October. - The decision does not cover copies already out there. A Korean-language translation appeared on GitHub on Oct. 7, 2026, a day before the announcement. Kim Dong-young davekim0807@ajupress. com. Copyright ⓒ Aju Press All rights reserved.
